question: Define 'public nuisance' under Section 270 of the BNS. How is it punished, and how does it differ from a private nuisance?
modelAnswer: Under s.270 (formerly s.268 IPC), a person is guilty of a public nuisance who does any act, or is guilty of an illegal omission, which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity, or which must necessarily cause injury, obstruction, danger or annoyance to persons who may have occasion to use any public right. The section adds that a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage. The ingredients are: (1) an act or illegal omission; (2) causing common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to people in the vicinity, or necessarily causing injury, obstruction, danger or annoyance to persons using a public right. Section 270 is only a definition. A public nuisance not otherwise punishable is punished under s.292 with fine up to ₹1,000 (non-cognizable, bailable). Repeating or continuing a public nuisance after being enjoined by a public servant with lawful authority is punishable under s.293 with simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both (cognizable). Many specific forms of nuisance — spreading disease, adulteration, fouling water, rash driving and so on — have their own sections (ss.271-291). A private nuisance, by contrast, affects only a particular individual or a few persons in the enjoyment of their property; it is a civil wrong remedied by a suit, not a crime under s.270. The key difference is that a public nuisance affects the public or the community in common. Magistrates can also act against public nuisances through conditional orders under BNSS s.152.

question: Explain the offences relating to the spread of infectious diseases and quarantine under Sections 271, 272 and 273.
modelAnswer: Section 271 (formerly s.269 IPC) punishes whoever unlawfully or negligently does any act which is, and which he knows or has reason to believe to be, likely to spread the infection of any disease dangerous to life, with imprisonment of either description up to six months, or fine, or both. Section 272 (formerly s.270 IPC) punishes the same conduct when done malignantly — deliberately, with a bad motive — with up to two years, or fine, or both. In both, the act must actually be likely to spread infection of a disease dangerous to life, and the accused must know or have reason to believe so; no one need in fact be infected. Both are cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. Section 273 (formerly s.271 IPC) punishes whoever knowingly disobeys a rule made by the Government for putting any mode of transport into quarantine, for regulating intercourse with such transport in quarantine, or for regulating intercourse between places where an infectious disease prevails and other places, with up to six months, or fine, or both; it is non-cognizable and bailable. The BNS widens s.273 to 'any mode of transport' in place of the IPC's reference to vessels. These sections were widely invoked during the COVID-19 pandemic under their IPC numbers, alongside s.188 IPC (now s.223 BNS) for breach of lockdown orders.

question: Discuss the offences relating to adulteration of food and drugs under Sections 274 to 278 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: Food: s.274 punishes whoever adulterates any article of food or drink so as to make it noxious as food or drink, intending to sell it as food or drink or knowing it likely to be sold as such, with up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. Section 275 punishes selling, or offering or exposing for sale, as food or drink any article that has been rendered or has become noxious or is unfit for consumption, knowing or having reason to believe it is noxious — same punishment. For food, the adulteration must make the article noxious (harmful); merely mixing in a cheaper harmless substance is not enough under s.274. Drugs: s.276 punishes adulterating a drug or medical preparation so as to lessen its efficacy, change its operation, or make it noxious, intending or knowing it likely to be sold or used for a medicinal purpose as if unadulterated, with up to one year, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. For drugs, reducing efficacy or changing the operation is enough — harm need not be shown. Section 277 punishes knowingly selling, exposing for sale, or issuing from a dispensary an adulterated drug as unadulterated, or causing an unaware person to use it medicinally — up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. Section 278 punishes knowingly selling or issuing a drug or preparation as a different drug or preparation — up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. All are non-cognizable; ss.274, 275, 277 and 278 are bailable, but s.276 is non-bailable. In practice these offences are often prosecuted together with, or under, special laws such as the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which carry heavier penalties.

question: What is rash or negligent driving under Section 281? How does it relate to Sections 106 and 125?
modelAnswer: Section 281 (formerly s.279 IPC) punishes whoever drives any vehicle, or rides, on any public way in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person, with imprisonment of either description up to six months, or fine up to ₹1,000, or both. It is cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. The ingredients are: (1) driving a vehicle or riding; (2) on a public way; (3) in a rash or negligent manner; (4) such as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury. 'Rash' means acting with awareness of the risk but indifference to it; 'negligent' means failing to take the care a reasonable person would take. The essence is the dangerous manner of driving — no accident or injury is required. If the rash or negligent act results in hurt or grievous hurt, s.125 (act endangering life or personal safety of others) applies, with higher punishments. If it causes death, s.106 (causing death by negligence) applies — up to five years and fine; s.106(2), which provides up to ten years and fine where the driver escapes without reporting the accident, has not yet been brought into force. Section 281 is therefore the basic offence of dangerous driving, and the other sections apply according to the harm actually caused. It is often charged together with offences under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

question: Explain the common pattern of Sections 286 to 291 (negligent conduct with dangerous things).
modelAnswer: Sections 286-291 (formerly ss.284-289 IPC) each deal with a particular source of danger: s.286 poisonous substances, s.287 fire or combustible matter, s.288 explosive substances, s.289 machinery, s.290 pulling down, repairing or constructing buildings, and s.291 animals. Sections 286-289 each have two limbs: (1) doing an act with the dangerous thing so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or be likely to cause hurt or injury to any person; and (2) knowingly or negligently omitting to take such order with the dangerous thing in one's possession (or care) as is sufficient to guard against any probable danger to human life from it. Section 290 has only the omission limb: knowingly or negligently failing, while demolishing, repairing or constructing a building, to take sufficient measures against probable danger to human life from its fall. Section 291 also has only the omission limb: knowingly or negligently failing to take sufficient measures with an animal in one's possession to guard against probable danger to human life or of grievous hurt. The punishment is the same across the group — imprisonment of either description up to six months, or fine, or both — with a fine limit of ₹5,000, except s.287 (fire), where it is ₹2,000. All are bailable and triable by any Magistrate; ss.289 and 290 are non-cognizable, and the rest cognizable. These are offences of creating danger; if death or injury results, ss.106 or 125 may also apply.

question: Discuss the law on obscenity under Section 294 of the BNS. What are the exceptions?
modelAnswer: Section 294(1) defines when material is obscene for the purposes of sub-section (2): a book, pamphlet, paper, writing, drawing, painting, representation, figure or any other object, including display of any content in electronic form, is deemed obscene if it is lascivious, or appeals to the prurient interest, or if its effect (or the effect of any one of its distinct items), taken as a whole, tends to deprave and corrupt persons who are likely, in all the circumstances, to read, see or hear it. Section 294(2) punishes whoever: (a) sells, hires out, distributes, publicly exhibits or circulates obscene material, or makes, produces or possesses it for those purposes; (b) imports, exports or conveys it for those purposes; (c) takes part in or profits from a business dealing in it; (d) advertises that anyone is engaged in such an act or that such material can be obtained; or (e) offers or attempts any of these. On first conviction the punishment is imprisonment of either description up to two years and fine up to ₹5,000; on a second or subsequent conviction, up to five years and fine up to ₹10,000. It is cognizable and bailable. The Exception excludes: (a) material whose publication is proved to be justified for the public good as being in the interest of science, literature, art, learning or other objects of general concern, or which is kept or used bona fide for religious purposes; and (b) representations on ancient monuments within the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, or in temples, on idol-cars, or kept or used for religious purposes. The courts judge obscenity by reading the work as a whole and by contemporary community standards, not by isolated passages. The BNS change is the express inclusion of electronic content. Obscene material online can also attract ss.67-67B of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

question: Distinguish between Section 294, Section 295 and Section 296 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: All three deal with obscenity, but they target different conduct. Section 294 punishes commercial or public dealing in obscene material — selling, hiring out, distributing, exhibiting, circulating, producing, possessing for those purposes, importing, exporting, advertising, or profiting from such a business — with two years and fine up to ₹5,000 on first conviction, and five years and fine up to ₹10,000 on subsequent conviction. It has exceptions for the public good, religious use, and monuments and temples. Section 295 is an aggravated form where the obscene object is sold, hired, distributed, exhibited or circulated to a child (a person under eighteen), or where this is offered or attempted: three years and fine up to ₹2,000 on first conviction; seven years and fine up to ₹5,000 on subsequent conviction. Section 296 is about conduct rather than material: doing an obscene act in a public place, or singing, reciting or uttering obscene songs, ballads or words in or near a public place, to the annoyance of others — up to three months, or fine up to ₹1,000, or both. Annoyance to others is an essential element of s.296. All three are cognizable and bailable, triable by any Magistrate.

question: Problem: A builder demolishing an old building on a busy road puts up no barricades. Debris piled on the road is left unlit at night. A falling brick injures a passer-by, and a motorcyclist crashes into the debris at night. Discuss the builder's liability under Chapter XV.
modelAnswer: Section 290: while pulling down a building, the builder knowingly or negligently omitted to take sufficient measures (barricades, nets) to guard against probable danger to human life from the fall of the building or part of it. This is an offence under s.290: up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both (non-cognizable, bailable). Section 285: by leaving debris on the public road unlit — an omission to take order with property in his charge — he caused danger, obstruction or injury to persons on a public way, which is punishable under s.285 with fine up to ₹5,000 (cognizable, bailable). Public nuisance: the obstruction of a public road also falls within the definition in s.270, but since it is specifically punishable under s.285, s.292 (which applies only where the nuisance is not otherwise punishable) would not be used. Beyond Chapter XV: because the passer-by was hurt by a falling brick and the motorcyclist was injured, the builder may also be liable under s.125 (act endangering life or personal safety of others) — s.125(a) where hurt is caused and s.125(b) where grievous hurt is caused. If anyone had died, s.106 (causing death by negligence) would apply. The builder may also face civil liability and action under municipal building regulations.

question: Problem: During an epidemic of a dangerous infectious disease, X, who has tested positive and been directed to home isolation, attends a crowded wedding. Y, also infected and angry at restrictions, deliberately spits on people at a market. Discuss their liability.
modelAnswer: X: by attending a crowded wedding while infected and under isolation directions, X negligently (or unlawfully) did an act likely to spread the infection of a disease dangerous to life, and, having tested positive, he knew or had reason to believe it was likely to spread the infection. He is liable under s.271: up to six months, or fine, or both. If the isolation direction was a lawfully promulgated order, X may also be liable under s.223 (disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant), which applies where disobedience causes or tends to cause danger to human life, health or safety — up to one year, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. Y: spitting on people deliberately while infected, out of anger, is a malignant act likely to spread infection of a disease dangerous to life, done with knowledge of that likelihood. Y is liable under s.272: up to two years, or fine, or both. Depending on the facts, Y may also be liable for assault or use of criminal force (spitting on a person can amount to criminal force). Both ss.271 and 272 are cognizable and bailable, and no one need actually have been infected for the offences to be complete.

question: Explain Section 283 (exhibition of false light, mark or buoy) and Section 284 (conveying persons in unsafe vessels).
modelAnswer: Section 283 (formerly s.281 IPC) punishes whoever exhibits any false light, mark or buoy, intending or knowing it likely that the exhibition will mislead any navigator. Because it can cause shipwrecks and loss of life, it is one of the most serious offences in the Chapter: imprisonment of either description up to seven years, and fine which shall not be less than ₹10,000 — both are mandatory. It is cognizable, bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. The ingredients are exhibiting a false light, mark or buoy, and intention or knowledge that it is likely to mislead a navigator; the navigator need not in fact be misled. Section 284 (formerly s.282 IPC) punishes whoever knowingly or negligently conveys, or causes to be conveyed for hire, any person by water in a vessel that is in such a state or so loaded as to endanger that person's life: up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both; cognizable, bailable, triable by any Magistrate. The ingredients are: conveying a person by water for hire; in a vessel so unsafe or overloaded as to endanger his life; knowingly or negligently. It targets unsafe and overcrowded ferries and boats. If a boat capsizes and passengers die, s.106 (causing death by negligence) may also apply.
